title: Groups where everyone reaches everyone
hook: Seven towns, one-way roads, one map. How many groups can all reach each other?

knows: depth-first search: follow a road as far as you can, then back up
one-way edges can give an order (which-order-is-allowed)
doesNotKnow: that a one-way graph splits into groups where everyone can reach everyone
Kosaraju's two passes: finish order, then the reversed graph
that the groups themselves form an ordering

misconception: In a graph with one-way roads, a town reachable from another is in the same cluster.
objective: The learner can explain that a group needs reaching both ways, so the 7-town map splits into 3 groups ({1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7}) even though 3 reaches 4, and that two depth-first passes (finish order, then the reversed roads from the last to finish) find them.

claims.text: With one-way roads 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1, 3 to 4, 4 to 5, 5 to 6, 6 to 4, 7 to 6, there are 3 groups where every town can reach every other: {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6} and {7}.
claims.source: Builder's node script (2026-10-14): brute-force reachability from every town, grouping towns that reach each other both ways, gives [1,2,3], [4,5,6], [7]; Kosaraju (Demo.tsx GROUPS) gives the same three.

claims.text: Pass 1, a depth-first search from town 1 (smaller towns and roads first), finishes the towns in the order 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 7 (shown as 1st to 7th).
claims.source: Demo.tsx FINISH: DFS over towns 1..7 in order, out-roads sorted ascending; builder's node script: discovery 1-6 at times 1-6, finish 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 at times 7-12, then 7 (times 13, 14). The order depends on the start town and neighbour order chosen (a convention); any DFS order gives the same groups.

claims.text: Pass 2 reverses every road and floods from the uncoloured town that finished last: from 7 it reaches only {7}; from 1, {1, 2, 3}; from 4, {4, 5, 6}, with 3 and 7 already coloured. Every reversed road leaving a new group led into a town already coloured (4 to 3, 6 to 7), so each flood stayed inside its own group.
claims.source: Demo.tsx GROUPS (flood over REVERSED in decreasing finish order); builder's node script gives starts 7, 1, 4 and groups [7], [1,2,3], [4,5,6]; the only reversed roads leaving a group are 4 to 3 and 6 to 7, both into coloured towns. Kosaraju's method and its correctness: CLRS 4e section 20.5 (STRONGLY-CONNECTED-COMPONENTS and its correctness theorem; builder did not check the lemma numbers).

claims.text: Every town is on one map, but town 3 can reach 4 and 4 cannot reach back, so the two loops are different groups. Town 7 reaches the right loop, and nothing reaches 7, so it is a group on its own.
claims.source: Ignoring direction, a search from town 1 reaches all 7 towns (builder's node script). With direction, reach(4) = {4, 5, 6} excludes 3; no road ends at 7, so reach-back to 7 is impossible from any other town.

claims.text: Shrinking each group to a point leaves 7 → {4, 5, 6} ← {1, 2, 3}: no loops left. That is why the groups can be put in order.
claims.source: The only roads between groups are 3 to 4 and 7 to 6 (builder's node script), giving the shrunk graph above with no cycle. In general the component graph is a directed acyclic graph: CLRS 4e section 20.5 (lemma that the component graph is acyclic; number not checked by the builder), so it has a topological order (CLRS 4e section 20.4).

recall.question: One-way roads: A to B, B to A, B to C. Which towns are in the same group, where everyone can reach everyone?
options: A and B; C is a group on its own
A, B and C, since all are connected
None: every town is its own group
recall.why: A and B reach each other both ways. B reaches C, but C cannot reach back, so C is not in their group, however close it is.
